about: Peace Lab data. Each node is one approach to fostering, cultivating, sustaining and developing peace, with a playable mini-prototype (play.engine). conf: 'ok' = the URL was opened and supports the claim on the card; 'check' = not yet confirmed, shown with a 'check source' flag. Verified 2026-10-13: DOIs via Crossref metadata, pages via a batched fetch of title and key text.

nodes.name: Compassion training
nodes.what: Short daily practice of wishing others well, starting with loved ones and widening to strangers and adversaries.
nodes.why: In a randomized study, two weeks of online compassion training increased altruistic giving to a stranger, with matching changes in brain responses to suffering.
nodes.mvp: A 7-minute daily guided audio plus a one-tap log of one kind act; compare giving in a simple game before and after.
nodes.q: Who is the hardest person for you to wish well, and what changes in your body when you try?

params.phrase: May you be safe. May you be free of suffering.

nodes.name: Deep canvassing
nodes.what: A ten-minute, non-judgmental conversation in which people recall their own experience of being judged, then reconsider an outgroup.
nodes.why: A door-to-door field experiment found attitude change that lasted at least three months.
nodes.mvp: A script card and a role-play partner; measure warmth toward the other group before, right after and one month later.
nodes.q: When were you last treated as 'one of them'? What did you need then?

params.topic: a group you find hard to understand

nodes.name: Perspective-getting
nodes.what: Instead of imagining what the other side thinks (perspective-taking), ask them and listen.
nodes.why: Across many experiments, imagining another's view did not make people more accurate about it; actually asking did.
nodes.mvp: Write your guess of a counterpart's view, then ask them three open questions and score how close you were.
nodes.q: Whose mind do you claim to know without ever having asked?

params.topic: how a typical person in another power sees your country

nodes.name: Intellectual humility
nodes.what: Holding beliefs with a confidence that matches the evidence, and being open to being wrong.
nodes.why: People higher in intellectual humility were less certain their own beliefs were correct and less inclined to call politicians who changed their minds 'flip-floppers'.
nodes.mvp: A weekly 'where might I be wrong?' log with a confidence number per belief.
nodes.q: Which of your political beliefs would you bet the least money on?

nodes.name: The overview effect
nodes.what: The shift astronauts describe on seeing Earth whole: borders vanish and the planet looks fragile.
nodes.why: Analysis of astronaut accounts links the experience to awe and self-transcendence.
nodes.mvp: A 3-minute 'Earth from orbit' contemplation before a negotiation; ask negotiators to note one shared stake.
nodes.q: If you saw your country's border from orbit, which line would you redraw first, and why?

params.prompt: Describe the Earth as if you had just seen it whole for the first time.

nodes.src: Yaden et al. 2016, Psychology of Consciousness

nodes.name: Loving-kindness (mettā)
nodes.what: An ancient Buddhist practice of radiating goodwill to all beings without exception.
nodes.why: The Karaniya Metta Sutta: 'Even as a mother protects with her life her child, her only child, so with a boundless heart should one cherish all living beings.'
nodes.mvp: Pair the verse with a 5-minute breathing timer; end by naming one person you find difficult.
nodes.q: What would 'without exception' mean for how you speak about a rival country?

params.phrase: May all beings be at ease.

nodes.name: Intergroup contact
nodes.what: Structured time together between members of groups in tension.
nodes.why: A meta-analysis of 515 studies (713 samples) found contact typically reduces prejudice; Allport's conditions (equal status, common goals, cooperation, institutional support) strengthen the effect.
nodes.mvp: A shared task, such as a repair or a meal, for 6 people from two groups, run under Allport's conditions; survey before and after.
nodes.q: Which group do you have almost no contact with, and what shared task could bring you together?

params.prompt: Design one meeting between two groups that meets Allport's four conditions.

nodes.name: Superordinate goals (Robbers Cave)
nodes.what: Rival groups cooperate when they face a goal neither can reach alone.
nodes.why: In Sherif's field study, hostility between two rival groups of boys eased once they faced goals that needed both groups to reach.
nodes.mvp: List problems no single power can solve alone, and draft the smallest joint step on one.
nodes.q: What is today's broken water tank that no power can fix alone?
nodes.src: Sherif et al. 1954/1961 (Classics in the History of Psychology)

nodes.name: Nonviolent Communication
nodes.what: Speak in observations, feelings, needs and requests instead of judgments.
nodes.why: A widely taught method for de-escalating conflict in families, schools and mediation.
nodes.mvp: Rewrite one hostile headline or message as observation, feeling, need and request.
nodes.q: What need is behind the last angry thing you said about another country?

params.prompt: Take a judgment you hold about another country. Rewrite it as: observation, feeling, need, request.

nodes.name: Educational exchange
nodes.what: Students and scholars living and working in another country for a year or more.
nodes.why: Long-running exchange programmes such as Fulbright build personal networks that outlast political cycles.
nodes.mvp: A pen-pal or virtual lab pairing two classrooms in different powers for one term.
nodes.q: Who from another country changed how you think, and how did you meet?

params.prompt: Design a one-term exchange between two classrooms in rival powers. What would they build together?

nodes.name: Sister cities
nodes.what: Formal, long-term ties between towns in different countries.
nodes.why: City-to-city links can keep people-to-people contact alive when national relations freeze.
nodes.mvp: Find your town's sister cities; send one letter or join one exchange.
nodes.q: What would your town share with a town in a rival power?

params.prompt: Pick a city in another power. List three things your two cities share.

nodes.name: Sustained dialogue
nodes.what: The same small group meets repeatedly over months or years to transform relationships, not just solve problems.
nodes.why: The Sustained Dialogue Institute trains campus and community groups in the method; it traces its roots to long-running US–Soviet citizen dialogues.
nodes.mvp: A five-session dialogue circle with a fixed group and a shared log.
nodes.q: Which relationship in your life would change if you met monthly for a year?

params.topic: a long-running dispute between two powers

nodes.name: Track 2 diplomacy (Pugwash)
nodes.what: Unofficial talks between experts and former officials that test ideas governments cannot yet float.
nodes.why: The Pugwash Conferences and Joseph Rotblat shared the 1995 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to reduce the role of nuclear arms.
nodes.mvp: Run a 90-minute tabletop with three 'delegations' on one flashpoint; record off-ramps.
nodes.q: What idea would you test quietly if no one could quote you?

nodes.name: Restorative justice
nodes.what: Bringing those harmed and those responsible together to repair harm, not only to punish.
nodes.why: The UN Office on Drugs and Crime publishes a handbook on designing restorative justice programmes.
nodes.mvp: A restorative circle script for one real conflict in a school or workplace.
nodes.q: What would repair look like for a harm your country has done?

params.prompt: Name a harm. Who was affected, what do they need, and whose obligation is it?

nodes.src: UNODC Handbook on Restorative Justice Programmes, 2nd ed. 2020

nodes.name: Virtual exchange
nodes.what: Facilitated online dialogue between students across political and cultural divides.
nodes.why: Organizations such as Soliya run facilitated cross-cultural dialogue at university scale.
nodes.mvp: A four-week facilitated video dialogue between two classes.
nodes.q: What would you ask a student your age in a rival power?

params.topic: what students in another power worry about

nodes.name: Music across divides
nodes.what: Ensembles that bring together musicians from communities in conflict.
nodes.why: Founded by Daniel Barenboim, the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra brings together musicians from communities in conflict.
nodes.mvp: Compose a melody that mixes two traditions, such as a pentatonic line over a minor progression.
nodes.q: What would an orchestra sound like if no two instruments played the same melody?

params.prompt: Describe a piece of music that combines two traditions you know.

nodes.name: Olympic Truce
nodes.what: An ancient Greek tradition of pausing hostilities for the Games, revived by the IOC and UN General Assembly resolutions.
nodes.why: A shared calendar ritual creates a recurring window for de-escalation.
nodes.mvp: Pick one recurring event and propose a 'truce week' around it.
nodes.q: Which shared ritual could pause a conflict you care about?

params.prompt: Design a truce ritual tied to a shared event.

nodes.name: Harmony without uniformity (和而不同)
nodes.what: Confucius: 'The gentleman seeks harmony but not sameness; the petty person seeks sameness but not harmony' (Analects 13.23).
nodes.why: A classical frame for coexistence that does not require agreement.
nodes.mvp: Write one rule for coexisting with a rival that does not require either side to change its values.
nodes.q: What would harmony without sameness look like between your country and its rival?

params.prompt: Describe a relationship where difference made it stronger.

nodes.name: Ubuntu
nodes.what: A Southern African ethic often summed up as 'a person is a person through other persons'.
nodes.why: South Africa's 1993 interim constitution named 'a need for ubuntu but not for victimisation' as a basis for reconciliation.
nodes.mvp: A circle where each person names how someone else made them who they are.
nodes.q: Who are you through?

params.prompt: List five people from other groups who made you who you are.

nodes.src: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa Act 200 of 1993, epilogue

nodes.name: Ahimsa (non-harm)
nodes.what: The Indian principle of non-harm in thought, word and deed, central to Gandhi's satyagraha.
nodes.why: Gandhi turned a personal ethic of non-harm into a method of mass political action.
nodes.mvp: A one-day 'no harm in word' practice: note every harsh word you notice yourself about to say.
nodes.q: Where does harm begin: in the act, the word, or the thought?

params.prompt: Track one day of your words. Where did harm start?

nodes.name: Hongik ingan (弘益人間)
nodes.what: 'Broadly benefit humanity', a founding ideal from Korean myth.
nodes.why: Reported as the stated ideal in Article 2 of Korea's Framework Act on Education.
nodes.mvp: Write a one-sentence 'benefit all humanity' test for one policy you care about.
nodes.q: Who is left out when a policy benefits 'our people'?

params.prompt: Apply 'broadly benefit humanity' to one national policy. What changes?

nodes.name: мир = peace = world
nodes.what: In Russian, мир means both 'peace' and 'world'.
nodes.why: Words for peace carry different pictures: harmony, calm, wholeness, a level field.
nodes.mvp: Learn one word for 'peace' a week, with its literal meaning.
nodes.q: If 'peace' and 'world' were the same word in your language, what would change?

nodes.name: Positive peace (Galtung)
nodes.what: Peace is not only the absence of direct violence (negative peace) but also the absence of structural violence (positive peace).
nodes.why: Galtung's 1969 article set the frame that most peace research still uses.
nodes.mvp: List the structural violence that would remain if all wars stopped tomorrow.
nodes.q: If wars stopped tomorrow, what violence would remain?

params.prompt: If every war stopped tomorrow, what violence would remain? List three kinds.

nodes.name: Education for peace
nodes.what: Teaching conflict skills, human rights and international understanding in schools.
nodes.why: UNESCO member states adopted a revised Recommendation on Education for Peace, Human Rights and Sustainable Development in 2023.
nodes.mvp: One lesson plan: two textbooks' accounts of the same event, side by side.
nodes.q: What did your school teach you about your country's rivals?

params.prompt: Recall how your schoolbooks described a rival country. What was left out?

nodes.src: UNESCO Recommendation on Education for Peace and Human Rights (2023)

nodes.name: Long-term thinking
nodes.what: Taking the next 10,000 years as the frame for decisions.
nodes.why: The Long Now Foundation builds projects, such as a 10,000-year clock, to stretch our sense of time.
nodes.mvp: A 1000-year audit: what in today's dispute will matter in the year 3000?
nodes.q: What part of today's rivalry will anyone remember in 1000 years?

params.prompt: Run a 1000-year audit on one current conflict.

nodes.name: Places of memory
nodes.what: Museums and memorials that keep the human cost of war present.
nodes.why: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum documents the atomic bombing and its victims.
nodes.mvp: Visit or study one place of memory and write what it asks of you.
nodes.q: What memorial does your country not yet have?

params.prompt: Describe a memorial you would build, and for whom.

nodes.name: Economic interdependence
nodes.what: Trade and financial ties that raise the cost of conflict.
nodes.why: The evidence is mixed: ties can bind, but Farrell and Newman show how network hubs can also be weaponized for coercion.
nodes.mvp: Map one supply chain across the powers: who could cut whom off?
nodes.q: Does depending on each other make us safer, or just more exposed?

params.prompt: Trace one object you own across the powers. Where is the chokepoint?

nodes.name: Shared infrastructure (Indus Waters)
nodes.what: Treaties that share a river, grid or pipeline between rivals.
nodes.why: The 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, brokered by the World Bank, divided a river system between India and Pakistan. Check its current status before citing it as a success.
nodes.mvp: Sketch one piece of infrastructure two rivals could co-own.
nodes.q: What would two rivals have to share to make war too costly?
nodes.src: World Bank fact sheet: the Indus Waters Treaty 1960

nodes.name: Counting the cost of violence
nodes.what: Estimating what violence costs and what peace spending buys.
nodes.why: The Institute for Economics and Peace publishes the Global Peace Index and estimates of the economic impact of violence.
nodes.mvp: A Fermi estimate: the cost of violence against spending on peace.
nodes.q: What would you do with a tenth of the world's military spending?
nodes.src: Institute for Economics and Peace: Vision of Humanity

nodes.name: Governing the commons
nodes.what: Communities can manage shared resources without either privatization or central control.
nodes.why: Elinor Ostrom was awarded the 2009 economics prize for her analysis of how communities govern shared resources.
nodes.mvp: Apply Ostrom-style rules (clear boundaries, local rule-making, monitoring, graduated sanctions) to one shared resource.
nodes.q: What commons do the great powers share, and who monitors it?

params.prompt: Pick a global commons. Who sets the rules, who monitors, and what are the sanctions?

nodes.name: Mediation
nodes.what: A trusted third party helps parties find an agreement.
nodes.why: UN Peacemaker collects peace agreements and mediation guidance.
nodes.mvp: Walk an escalation ladder and mark where a mediator could step in.
nodes.q: Who could both sides of a conflict you care about trust as a go-between?

nodes.name: Women in peace processes
nodes.what: Including women as negotiators, mediators and signatories.
nodes.why: An IPI study reports that agreements are 35% more likely to last 15 years when women participate in their creation (citing Stone's statistical analysis).
nodes.mvp: Audit one peace process: who was at the table?
nodes.q: Who is missing from the table in the conflict you follow most?

params.prompt: Pick a negotiation. List who was at the table, then who was not.

nodes.src: O'Reilly, Ó Súilleabháin & Paffenholz 2015, Reimagining Peacemaking (IPI)

refs.label: UN Women: facts and figures on women, peace and security

nodes.name: UN Peacebuilding Commission
nodes.what: An intergovernmental advisory body that supports countries emerging from conflict.
nodes.why: Peace often fails in the years after a deal; the Commission exists to keep attention on that phase.
nodes.mvp: Pick one post-conflict country and list what would need to hold for ten years.
nodes.q: Who keeps paying attention once the cameras leave?

params.prompt: What would need to hold for ten years after a peace deal?

nodes.name: International Court of Justice
nodes.what: The UN's principal judicial organ settles disputes between states.
nodes.why: Courts turn disputes into arguments over rules instead of force.
nodes.mvp: Read one ICJ case summary and note what each side argued.
nodes.q: Which dispute would you most like to see settled by a court instead?

params.prompt: Draft the question you would ask the Court to decide in one dispute.

nodes.name: Citizens' assemblies
nodes.what: A randomly selected group of citizens deliberates and recommends.
nodes.why: Ireland's Citizens' Assemblies have deliberated on divisive questions and made recommendations to parliament.
nodes.mvp: Draft a statement both sides could sign, then test it for loaded words.
nodes.q: Would you trust 100 randomly chosen people from both sides to draft a deal?

nodes.name: Truth commissions
nodes.what: Public processes that record what happened and acknowledge victims.
nodes.why: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission is the best-known example.
nodes.mvp: Write the one sentence of acknowledgement you would want from the other side.
nodes.q: What truth would your country find hardest to tell?

params.prompt: Write the acknowledgement you would want to hear, then the one you would owe.

nodes.src: South Africa: Truth and Reconciliation Commission

nodes.name: Perpetual peace (Kant)
nodes.what: Kant's 1795 sketch: republics, a federation of free states, and universal hospitality.
nodes.why: It anticipated the democratic peace debate and international institutions.
nodes.mvp: Design rules for the US–China–Russia relationship from behind a veil.
nodes.q: What would universal hospitality ask of your country's border?

nodes.name: Veil of ignorance (Rawls)
nodes.what: Choose rules without knowing which position you will occupy.
nodes.why: The original position is a standard tool for testing fairness.
nodes.mvp: Write rules for the great-power relationship, then get assigned a country at random.
nodes.q: Which rule would you change if you might be born in the weakest country?
nodes.src: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Original Position

nodes.name: Confidence-building measures
nodes.what: Notifications, observations and data exchange on military activity.
nodes.why: The OSCE Vienna Document 2011 sets out confidence- and security-building measures among participating states.
nodes.mvp: A trust ledger: log small unilateral steps and whether they were returned.
nodes.q: What one notification would make you less afraid of a rival's army?

nodes.name: GRIT: graduated reciprocation
nodes.what: Osgood's strategy: announce and carry out small unilateral conciliatory steps, inviting reciprocation.
nodes.why: In his 1963 'Strategy of Peace' speech, Kennedy declared the US would not conduct nuclear tests in the atmosphere so long as other states did not: a unilateral first step.
nodes.mvp: Log one small conciliatory step a week and whether it was returned.
nodes.q: What small step could you take first, without waiting?
nodes.src: Kennedy, Commencement Address at American University, 10 June 1963 (American Presidency Project)

nodes.name: Arms control with verification
nodes.what: Treaties that cap or eliminate weapons, with inspections to check.
nodes.why: Under the INF Treaty a total of 2,692 missiles were eliminated by 1991, with on-site inspections.
nodes.mvp: Design the smallest verifiable promise two rivals could make.
nodes.q: What is the smallest promise you could verify?

params.prompt: Draft the smallest verifiable promise between two rivals. How would each side check it?

nodes.name: Crisis hotlines
nodes.what: Direct links between leaders for use in a crisis.
nodes.why: The US and USSR agreed the Hot Line in June 1963, after the Cuban missile crisis.
nodes.mvp: Walk an escalation ladder: at which rung would you pick up the phone?
nodes.q: Who would you call first in a crisis, and do you have their number?
nodes.src: US State Department: Hot Line Agreement 1963

nodes.name: UN peacekeeping
nodes.what: Multinational forces deployed to protect civilians and support ceasefires.
nodes.why: Using monthly data on African civil wars from 1991 to 2008, more UN troops and police were associated with fewer civilian killings.
nodes.mvp: A Fermi estimate: how many peacekeepers for a region, and what would it cost?
nodes.q: What would it take for your country to send peacekeepers alongside a rival's?

nodes.name: Disarmament, demobilization, reintegration
nodes.what: Helping fighters lay down arms and return to civilian life.
nodes.why: Peace deals often fail if former fighters have no livelihood.
nodes.mvp: List what a former fighter would need in the first 100 days.
nodes.q: What would you need to put down a weapon?

params.prompt: List what a former fighter needs in the first 100 days.

nodes.name: Mine ban and demining
nodes.what: A treaty ban on anti-personnel mines, plus clearance and victim assistance.
nodes.why: Landmines keep killing long after wars end. Check which states parties have recently announced withdrawals.
nodes.mvp: Find one cleared minefield's story and what the land is used for now.
nodes.q: What weapons of today will still harm children in 50 years?

params.prompt: Which of today's weapons will still cause harm in 50 years?

nodes.name: Civil resistance
nodes.what: Strikes, boycotts, protests and non-cooperation instead of arms.
nodes.why: Across major campaigns from 1900 to 2006, nonviolent resistance was more than twice as effective as violent resistance in reaching its stated goals.
nodes.mvp: List the pillars of support for one policy you oppose, and one nonviolent way to shift each.
nodes.q: Which pillar of support would move first?

params.prompt: Map the pillars of support for one policy. How could each be shifted nonviolently?

nodes.src: Stephan & Chenoweth 2008, International Security; Chenoweth & Stephan 2011 (Columbia University Press)

nodes.name: War pre-mortem
nodes.what: Imagine the war has already happened, then work out why, and set tripwires and off-ramps.
nodes.why: Gary Klein's project pre-mortem helps teams find failure modes before they happen.
nodes.mvp: Walk an escalation ladder for one flashpoint with a tripwire and off-ramp at each rung.
nodes.q: It is five years from now and the war happened. What was the first missed off-ramp?
nodes.src: Klein 2007, Performing a Project Premortem, Harvard Business Review

nodes.name: Evolution of cooperation
nodes.what: In repeated games, cooperation can emerge between self-interested players.
nodes.why: In Axelrod's tournaments, tit-for-tat (nice, retaliatory, forgiving, clear) did well.
nodes.mvp: Play 10 rounds of the prisoner's dilemma against five strategies, then run the tournament.
nodes.q: What does 'forgiving' mean for a nation?

nodes.name: The stag hunt
nodes.what: Hunting a stag together pays more, but only if both trust; hunting hare alone is safe.
nodes.why: Skyrms' 2001 address, The Stag Hunt, makes the case that trust, not just self-interest, is the core problem of social cooperation.
nodes.mvp: Play the stag hunt for 10 rounds and watch how trust forms or breaks.
nodes.q: What is the stag the great powers could hunt together?
nodes.src: Skyrms 2001, The Stag Hunt, APA Proceedings

nodes.name: Conflict early warning
nodes.what: Forecasting where violence is likely, months ahead, from open data.
nodes.why: ViEWS publishes open-source forecasts of armed conflict.
nodes.mvp: Pick a forecast region and write what early action would look like.
nodes.q: If you knew a war was 70% likely next year, what would you do this month?

params.prompt: A forecast says conflict is likely in a region next year. What is the cheapest early action?

nodes.name: Open satellite verification
nodes.what: Open satellite imagery lets anyone check claims about troops, ships and damage.
nodes.why: The EU's Copernicus programme publishes free Earth-observation data.
nodes.mvp: Check one claim about a military build-up against open imagery.
nodes.q: What claim would you check first if you had a satellite?

params.prompt: Pick a claim in the news. What would satellite imagery need to show to confirm it?

nodes.name: Bridging-based ranking
nodes.what: Rank content by whether people who usually disagree both rate it helpful.
nodes.why: Community Notes (formerly Birdwatch) uses a bridging algorithm; Pol.is uses a similar idea to find consensus statements.
nodes.mvp: Write a statement both sides could sign and check it for loaded and shared-value words.
nodes.q: What could both sides of your sharpest disagreement sign?
nodes.src: Wojcik et al. 2022, Birdwatch: Crowd Wisdom and Bridging Algorithms (arXiv); Pol.is

nodes.name: Machine translation for all
nodes.what: Translation models covering 200 languages, including many low-resource ones.
nodes.why: The NLLB project scaled neural machine translation to 200 languages.
nodes.mvp: Read one article in another power's domestic press, machine-translated.
nodes.q: What would you read if every language were open to you?

nodes.name: AI safety cooperation
nodes.what: Joint evaluation and risk research on frontier AI.
nodes.why: At Bletchley Park in November 2023, countries including the US and China signed a declaration on AI safety.
nodes.mvp: Draft the smallest joint AI-safety step two rival labs could take.
nodes.q: What AI risk is no one country able to manage alone?

nodes.name: Cyber norms
nodes.what: Voluntary norms of responsible state behaviour in cyberspace, such as not attacking critical infrastructure.
nodes.why: The 2015 UN Group of Governmental Experts report (A/70/174) proposed voluntary norms.
nodes.mvp: Log reciprocated restraint steps in a trust ledger.
nodes.q: Which infrastructure should every power agree never to attack?

nodes.name: Open government
nodes.what: Governments co-create commitments with civil society on transparency and participation.
nodes.why: Transparency makes intentions easier to read, which lowers the cost of trust.
nodes.mvp: Pick one government dataset and check one claim against it.
nodes.q: What would you want a rival government to publish?

params.prompt: What one dataset would make you trust a rival government more?

nodes.name: SESAME synchrotron
nodes.what: A shared research light source in Jordan whose members include states with tense relations.
nodes.why: Science facilities give rivals a reason to sit at the same table for decades.
nodes.mvp: Name one instrument two rival powers could build and run together.
nodes.q: What would scientists from rival powers build if politics allowed?

nodes.name: Big science (CERN)
nodes.what: Large shared laboratories run by many countries.
nodes.why: CERN, running since 1954, is governed jointly by its member states and hosts scientists from around the world.
nodes.mvp: Sketch a shared lab for a problem the powers all face.
nodes.q: What question is big enough to need every power?

nodes.name: Planetary defense
nodes.what: Finding and deflecting asteroids that could hit Earth.
nodes.why: NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately hit the asteroid Dimorphos and altered its orbit: the first successful planetary-defense test.
nodes.mvp: Draft the joint protocol if an asteroid were found on a collision course.
nodes.q: Would a shared threat from space change how rivals treat each other?

nodes.name: Peace parks
nodes.what: Conservation areas that cross national borders.
nodes.why: The Peace Parks Foundation supports transfrontier conservation areas in southern Africa.
nodes.mvp: Find one border ecosystem and sketch a joint park.
nodes.q: Which animal migrates across the border you care about?

params.prompt: Pick a border. What lives on both sides, and who protects it?

nodes.name: Climate cooperation
nodes.what: Shared targets and transparency on emissions.
nodes.why: The Paris Agreement asks every party to set and report nationally determined contributions.
nodes.mvp: Draft one joint climate step for two rival powers.
nodes.q: Is the climate a shared enemy, or a new arena for rivalry?

nodes.name: Antarctic Treaty
nodes.what: A continent set aside for peace and science, with inspections.
nodes.why: Signed in Washington on 1 December 1959 by the twelve countries active in Antarctica, in the middle of the Cold War: 'Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only'.
nodes.mvp: Pick another commons (the Moon, the deep sea, the Arctic) and draft its first article.
nodes.q: What other place should belong to no one?

params.prompt: Draft Article 1 of a treaty for another commons.

nodes.name: Environmental peacebuilding
nodes.what: Using shared natural resources as a reason to cooperate, not compete.
nodes.why: The Environmental Peacebuilding Association connects research and practice on this.
nodes.mvp: Map one shared resource between two communities and one joint management step.
nodes.q: What natural resource could two rival communities manage together?

params.prompt: Name a shared resource between two rivals and one joint step.

nodes.name: Global seed vault
nodes.what: A backup of the world's crop diversity, deposited by gene banks from many countries.
nodes.why: Insurance that outlives any one government.
nodes.mvp: List what you would put in a vault for the year 3000.
nodes.q: What should humanity back up?

params.prompt: What would you put in a vault for the year 3000, and why?

nodes.name: Disaster diplomacy
nodes.what: Disasters can open windows for rivals to help each other, as after the 1999 earthquakes in Turkey and Greece.
nodes.why: Research on disaster diplomacy finds such windows real but usually short unless other ties exist.
nodes.mvp: Plan what your country would offer a rival after an earthquake.
nodes.q: Would you accept help from your rival after a disaster?

params.prompt: A rival suffers a disaster. What would your country offer, and how?

nodes.name: Health as a bridge
nodes.what: Joint campaigns against disease across political lines.
nodes.why: WHO's intensified smallpox eradication campaign began in 1967; eradication was certified in December 1979.
nodes.mvp: Pick one disease and list what each power would contribute.
nodes.q: What disease could the great powers end together?

nodes.name: News de-biaser: form your own opinion
nodes.what: Write your take first, then compare versions of a story: loaded words, unattributed claims, omissions and evidence rungs.
nodes.why: Short prebunking videos improved recognition of manipulation techniques (Roozenbeek et al. 2022). Professional fact-checkers read laterally, leaving a site to check who is behind it, while historians and students read vertically (Wineburg & McGrew 2019). Risk: in one field experiment, following opposing views made Republicans more conservative (Bail et al. 2018).
nodes.mvp: Paste 2–3 versions of a story and see the highlights and omission diff before revisiting your take.
nodes.q: What did you believe about this story before you read any version of it?

nodes.name: Accuracy nudge
nodes.what: Before sharing, ask: is this accurate?
nodes.why: Subtly shifting attention to accuracy improved the quality of news people shared, in surveys and a Twitter field experiment.
nodes.mvp: A 'how accurate is this?' prompt before each share for one week.
nodes.q: What did you share last week that you never checked?

nodes.name: Mirror headlines
nodes.what: Line up headlines from different outlets on the same event and compare tone.
nodes.why: Outlets differ measurably in slant; Groseclose and Milyo proposed one way to measure it.
nodes.mvp: Paste headlines from three outlets and compare loaded-word counts.
nodes.q: Which outlet's version did you believe first, and why?
nodes.src: Groseclose & Milyo 2005, Quarterly Journal of Economics

nodes.name: Read their domestic news
nodes.what: Read what another country's media tell their own public, translated, not what they tell foreigners.
nodes.why: The Reuters Institute Digital News Report shows how news use differs from country to country.
nodes.mvp: One translated domestic article a week from each of the three powers.
nodes.q: What does a rival's public hear about your country?

params.prompt: Read one translated domestic article from another power. What surprised you?

nodes.name: Slow news
nodes.what: Save a headline and your take now; revisit after a week to see what turned out to be true.
nodes.why: First reports are often wrong; a delay shows how much your view depended on them.
nodes.mvp: A 7-day revisit list for headlines.
nodes.q: Which of last month's headlines turned out wrong?

nodes.name: Opinion provenance
nodes.what: For each strongly held view, record where it came from on the evidence ladder (A–F).
nodes.why: Mercier and Sperber argue reasoning evolved to argue, so we are better at finding support for our views than at testing them.
nodes.mvp: A chart of your own views by evidence rung.
nodes.q: How many of your views rest on state media or a friend's say-so?
nodes.src: Mercier & Sperber 2011, Behavioral and Brain Sciences

nodes.name: Ideological Turing test
nodes.what: Can you state the other side's view so well that they would think you hold it?
nodes.why: Bryan Caplan proposed the test in 2011 as a measure of understanding.
nodes.mvp: Write the other side's view, score it on a rubric, then send it to a real person from that side.
nodes.q: Could you pass as the other side?

params.topic: a contested question between the powers

nodes.name: Omission diff
nodes.what: Find what one version of a story leaves out that another includes.
nodes.why: McCombs and Shaw showed media shape what the public thinks is important; what is omitted shapes it too.
nodes.mvp: Paste two versions of a story and list sentences missing from each.
nodes.q: What did your usual source leave out this week?

nodes.name: Trust ledger
nodes.what: Keep a record of small conciliatory acts and whether they were returned.
nodes.why: Lindskold reviewed the evidence on GRIT: how conciliatory acts, announced and carried out, affect trust in conflict.
nodes.mvp: A shared ledger for two groups, reviewed monthly.
nodes.q: What would your ledger with a rival look like this year?

words.lit: 和 harmony + 平 level, calm: peace, a state free of war
the same two characters in reverse order: peace, a peaceful situation; also calm
from the Sino-Korean 平和: peace, harmony
peace, well-being; also a greeting. Root s-l-m
peace; also hello and goodbye. Same Semitic root as salām

problems.name: Planetary defense
problems.why: An impactor does not check passports; detection needs telescopes on every longitude.

problems.name: Pandemic early warning
problems.why: Pathogen data has to be shared within days to matter.

problems.name: AI safety evaluations
problems.why: A dangerous capability found in one lab is a risk to all.

problems.name: Arctic search and rescue
problems.why: Ships and planes in the Arctic depend on whoever is closest.

problems.name: Nuclear accident response
problems.why: Fallout ignores borders; notification and assistance need standing channels.

problems.name: Space debris
problems.why: Every collision makes orbit more dangerous for everyone.

problems.name: Climate adaptation in shared river basins
problems.why: Glacier melt changes rivers that cross several borders.

problems.name: Antimicrobial resistance
problems.why: Resistant bacteria spread through trade, travel and food.

deck.title: Veil of ignorance
deck.setup: You will be born into one of the seven powers, in a random role: leader, soldier, farmer, student. Before you know which, you write the rules between them.
qs: Which rule would you insist on if you might be born in the weakest power?
Which current rule would you abolish?
What would you want to be true about borders?

deck.title: Stag hunt
deck.setup: Two hunters can each catch a hare alone, or catch a stag together, but only if both stay at their posts.
qs: What is the stag the great powers could hunt together?
What makes each side defect to the hare?
What signal would make you stay at your post?

deck.title: Forgiving nations
deck.setup: In repeated prisoner's dilemmas, strategies that forgive an occasional defection often do better than strategies that never forget.
qs: What does 'forgiving' mean for a nation?
How many defections should a nation forgive?
Who keeps score, and can the scorekeeper be trusted?

deck.title: Today's broken water tank
deck.setup: At Robbers Cave, rival groups made peace when the camp's water supply failed and they had to fix it together.
qs: What is today's broken water tank?
Who would have to carry the pipe?
What happens after it is fixed?

deck.title: Overview effect for leaders
deck.setup: Every head of state must spend a week in orbit before taking office.
qs: What would change in their first speech?
Which leader would change the most?
What would they miss seeing from up there?

deck.title: Swapped childhoods
deck.setup: Two rival leaders discover they were swapped at birth, each raised in the other's country.
qs: Which of their beliefs would stay the same?
What would each defend most fiercely?
What would they say to each other?

deck.title: мир = peace = world
deck.setup: In Russian one word, мир, means both 'peace' and 'world'.
qs: What if your language used one word for both?
Is peace a place or a state?
Which other word would you merge with 'peace'?

deck.title: A 1000-year audit
deck.setup: Historians in the year 3000 write one paragraph about today's great-power rivalry.
qs: What do they find absurd?
What do they praise?
What do they say we should have seen?

deck.title: Ship of Theseus for treaties
deck.setup: A treaty is amended clause by clause until no original text remains.
qs: Is it still the same treaty?
What must never change for it to stay itself?
Which treaty today is mostly replaced planks?

deck.title: Harmony without uniformity
deck.setup: An orchestra where no two instruments play the same melody, yet the piece works.
qs: What makes it music and not noise?
Who is the conductor, or is there none?
Which instrument is your country?

deck.title: Galtung's inversion
qs: What violence remains?
Who still suffers, and why?
Which of it could end within a decade?

deck.title: Universal hospitality
deck.setup: Kant proposed a right of every stranger not to be treated with hostility on arrival.
qs: What would that ask of your country's border?
What would it ask of you, at your door?
Where does hospitality end?

deck.title: Zero-sum audit
deck.setup: List every way the great powers compete, then mark which ones are truly zero-sum.
qs: How many are really zero-sum?
Which only look zero-sum?
Which could become positive-sum with one rule change?

deck.title: The empty chair
deck.setup: At every summit, one chair is left empty for future generations and other species.
qs: What would the chair say?
Who should speak for it?
What decision would it veto?

deck.title: The smallest verifiable promise
deck.setup: Two rivals may make only one promise this year, and it must be checkable by the other.
qs: What is the smallest promise worth making?
How would each side check it?
What would the second promise be?

deck.title: A Fermi estimate of peace work
deck.setup: Estimate how many people work full-time on peace today, and what would double it.
qs: What is your estimate, and how did you get it?
What counts as peace work?
What would double it in ten years?

loop.on: Mark a headline or node that caught you.
loop.off: Carry a small notebook; note one moment of tension or kindness each day.

loop.on: Answer the node's question in the journal.
loop.off: Walk for 10 minutes holding the question; steelman the other side.

loop.on: Collide two nodes from different domains.
loop.off: Talk to someone from another field and swap one idea.

loop.on: Compose an MVP from up to five nodes.
loop.off: Make one physical thing: a letter, a melody, a sketch, a meal.

loop.on: Run the MVP's smallest test and log it.
loop.off: Try it with one real person this week.
Share what you made with someone who disagrees with you.
Once a month, re-read your notes in a quiet place and re-rank the nodes.

daily.title: A minute of silence
daily.how: At a fixed time each day, stop for one minute of silence for those living through war.

daily.title: One word for peace
daily.how: Learn one word for 'peace' in another language, with its literal meaning.

daily.title: Steelman while walking
daily.how: On a walk, state an opposing view in its strongest form, out loud or in your head.

weekly.title: A meal or call across a divide
weekly.how: Share a meal or call with someone across a border or a political line. Ask: what do you fear, what do you hope?

weekly.title: Combine two traditions
weekly.how: Make something that combines two traditions, e.g. a melody in a pentatonic scale over a Russian minor progression.

weekly.title: Trace a supply chain
weekly.how: Trace one object you own across the powers: where was each part made?

monthly.title: A letter you won't send
monthly.how: Write a letter to a leader of another country. Keep it.

monthly.title: Run one small test
monthly.how: Run the smallest test from one MVP you composed, with a real person.

monthly.title: Visit a place of memory
monthly.how: Visit a memorial, museum or cemetery, and write what it asks of you.

yearly.title: Review the journal
yearly.how: Read the whole year's journal. What changed in you?

yearly.title: Re-rank the nodes
yearly.how: Rank the approaches again. Which moved up, and why?

yearly.title: Publish one piece
yearly.how: Publish one essay, song, talk or tool that came out of the year.
